text: Plato has set out two laws concerning the gods, and Genesis 6 becomes difficult when read beside them (Republic 379a–383c). Yahweh is grieved in his heart, and Yahweh resolves to destroy every living thing (Genesis 6:6–7). On Plato’s accounting, therefore, Yahweh is both moved and the cause of harm. Plato’s laws were written against gods who do evil from caprice, and the flood has a reason: the earth is filled with violence (Genesis 6:11). That reason narrows the conflict with Plato’s laws. It does not remove it. Plato allows a god to punish if the poet can show that the punishment is just, and if he can show that the one punished is made better by it (Republic 380b–c). No one is made better by a flood. Plato also forbids divine grief, since grief means change, and a good god cannot be affected by what is below him (Republic 381b–c). Genesis gives another account of goodness. God is affected by what his creatures have become, and his grief measures how seriously he takes their corruption. Noah and Socrates also arrive at theology at different points in their building. Noah builds under God’s judgment from the beginning, to dimensions given by the God who has looked at the world and been wounded by it (Genesis 6:14–16). Socrates derives his city from human need and reaches theology only when the guardians must be educated. Both readings read inner disorder on a larger scale: Genesis moves from every imagination of the human heart to an earth filled with violence, and Socrates looks for justice written larger in a city. When the readings break off, the ark is waiting for its passengers and Socrates’ city is waiting for its rulers.
